summary: Defines extensions to BGP-4 so it can carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols, such as IPv6. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4760.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP-4 could only describe routes in IPv4 terms. This RFC adds two optional pieces of information to a BGP update: one that says which destinations are reachable and which router to send traffic to next, and one that says which destinations are no longer reachable. A tag on each says which network protocol the addresses belong to.

questions: how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
subtitle: How BGP-4 learned to carry routes for IPv6 and other network protocols without breaking old routers.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 could only carry routing information for IPv4. Its next hop address, its aggregator attribute and its route prefixes were all written in IPv4 terms, and there was no way to say that a route concerned some other network layer protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Two new optional path attributes are added. MP_REACH_NLRI carries reachable destinations together with the next hop to use for them, and MP_UNREACH_NLRI carries destinations being withdrawn. Each names the address family it applies to, and both are non-transitive, so a router that does not understand them ignores them and does not pass them on.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2858 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4760.

today: RFC 2858 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4760.

sections.title: What in BGP-4 Was IPv4-Specific
sections.content:
The RFC notes that only three pieces of information carried by BGP-4 are IPv4 specific: the NEXT_HOP attribute, which is expressed as an IPv4 address; the AGGREGATOR attribute, which contains an IPv4 address; and the NLRI, which is expressed as IPv4 address prefixes. The document assumes that any BGP speaker, including one that supports the multiprotocol capabilities it defines, has to have an IPv4 address, which is used among other things in the AGGREGATOR attribute.

To let BGP-4 support routing for multiple network layer protocols, only two things have to be added: the ability to associate a particular network layer protocol with the next hop information, and the ability to associate a particular network layer protocol with the NLRI. Individual network layer protocols are identified using Address Family, as defined in RFC 1700.

The RFC adds an observation that shapes the design. Next hop information is meaningful only together with the advertisement of reachable destinations; with the advertisement of unreachable destinations it means nothing. That suggests grouping the advertisement of reachable destinations with the next hop to be used for them, and segregating the advertisement of unreachable destinations.

For backward compatibility, and to simplify the introduction of the capabilities, the document uses two new attributes, Multiprotocol Reachable NLRI (MP_REACH_NLRI) and Multiprotocol Unreachable NLRI (MP_UNREACH_NLRI). Both are optional and non-transitive, so a BGP speaker that does not support the multiprotocol capabilities simply ignores the information carried in them and does not pass it to other BGP speakers.
sections.plainLanguage: Only three parts of a BGP update were tied to IPv4. The fix adds a label saying which network protocol the addresses belong to, and puts reachable routes in one attribute and withdrawn routes in another so the next-hop address stays with the routes it applies to.

sections.title: The MP_REACH_NLRI Attribute
sections.content:
MP_REACH_NLRI is an optional non-transitive attribute with type code 14. It can be used to advertise a feasible route to a peer, to permit a router to advertise the network layer address of the router that should be used as the next hop to the destinations listed in the attribute, and to allow a router to report some or all of the Subnetwork Points of Attachment that exist within the local system.

The attribute carries an Address Family Identifier of 2 octets, a Subsequent Address Family Identifier of 1 octet, a Length of Next Hop Network Address of 1 octet, the Network Address of Next Hop in a variable length field, a Number of SNPAs of 1 octet with a length-prefixed SNPA field for each, and finally the Network Layer Reachability Information in a variable length field.

The next hop information defines the network layer address of the border router to be used as the next hop to the destinations listed in the attribute. A router may use one of its own interface addresses in the next hop component when advertising to an external peer, provided that peer shares a common subnet with the next hop address; this is known as a "first party" next hop. A "third party" next hop is one belonging to an internal peer router or to an external peer router, again provided the external peer shares a common subnet with the next hop address.

A BGP speaker must never advertise the address of a peer to that peer as a next hop for a route it is originating, and must never install a route with itself as the next hop. An UPDATE message that carries MP_REACH_NLRI must also carry the ORIGIN and AS_PATH attributes, in both EBGP and IBGP exchanges, and in IBGP exchanges it must also carry the LOCAL_PREF attribute. If such a message is received from an external peer, the local system checks that the leftmost AS in the AS_PATH equals the autonomous system number of the peer that sent it; if it does not, the local system sends a NOTIFICATION message with the UPDATE Message Error code and the Malformed AS_PATH subcode.
sections.plainLanguage: This attribute says which destinations are reachable, which router to send the traffic to next, and which network protocol the addresses use. A router must include the usual origin and path attributes alongside it, and must check that the path starts with the peer it came from.

sections.title: MP_UNREACH_NLRI and NLRI Encoding
sections.content:
MP_UNREACH_NLRI is an optional non-transitive attribute with type code 15, used for withdrawing multiple unfeasible routes from service. It carries an Address Family Identifier of 2 octets, a Subsequent Address Family Identifier of 1 octet, and a variable length field of withdrawn routes. An UPDATE message that contains MP_UNREACH_NLRI is not required to carry any other path attributes.

The network layer reachability information in both attributes is encoded as one or more 2-tuples of the form length, prefix. The Length field indicates the length in bits of the address prefix, and a length of zero indicates a prefix that matches all addresses in the address family, with a prefix itself of zero octets. The Prefix field contains an address prefix followed by enough trailing bits to make the end of the field fall on an octet boundary; the value of those trailing bits is irrelevant.

The RFC also specifies what happens when an attribute arrives broken. If a BGP speaker receives an UPDATE containing MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI and determines that the attribute is incorrect, it must delete all the BGP routes received from that neighbor whose AFI/SAFI is the same as the one carried in the incorrect attribute. For the duration of the BGP session over which the UPDATE was received, the speaker should then ignore all subsequent routes with that AFI/SAFI received over that session. It may also terminate the session, with the NOTIFICATION message code and subcode indicating Update Message Error and Optional Attribute Error.
sections.plainLanguage: The withdrawal attribute lists routes that are no longer reachable. The reachability information itself is a list of prefix lengths and prefixes. If a router receives a malformed attribute, it drops every route of that address family from that peer for the rest of the session.

sections.title: Address Family and Subsequent Address Family Identifiers
sections.content:
Both new attributes carry a pair of identifiers. The Address Family Identifier names the network layer protocol that the addresses in the attribute belong to, using the values specified in RFC 1700. The Subsequent Address Family Identifier gives additional information about the type of the network layer reachability information carried in the attribute.

The RFC defines three values for the Subsequent Address Family Identifier field: 1 for network layer reachability information used for unicast forwarding, 2 for information used for multicast forwarding, and 3 for information used for both unicast and multicast forwarding.

The IANA considerations section assigns the SAFI name space. SAFI value 0 is reserved. Values 1, 2 and 3 are assigned in this document. Values 4 through 63 are to be assigned by IANA using the IETF Consensus policy defined in RFC 2434. Values 64 through 127 are to be assigned using the First Come First Served policy defined in RFC 2434. Values 128 through 255 are for private use and are not to be assigned by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers travel with the attribute: one says which network protocol the addresses are, the other says whether the routes are for unicast, multicast, or both.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that uses the multiprotocol extensions should use the Capability Advertisement procedures to determine whether the peer could use them. The Capability Code is set to 1, which indicates multiprotocol extensions capabilities, and the Capability Length is set to 4. The Capability Value field is laid out as 16 bits of Address Family Identifier, 8 reserved bits that should be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and 8 bits of Subsequent Address Family Identifier, both encoded the same way as in the multiprotocol extensions themselves.

A speaker that supports multiple AFI, SAFI tuples includes them as multiple capabilities in the Capabilities Optional Parameter. To have a bi-directional exchange of routing information for a particular AFI, SAFI between a pair of BGP speakers, each speaker must advertise to the other, through the capability advertisement mechanism, the capability to support that particular AFI, SAFI.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending these routes, the two routers tell each other which address families they can handle. Both sides have to say so, or the exchange only works in one direction.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is one sentence long. It states that this extension to BGP does not change the underlying security issues inherent in the existing BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no new security problems of its own. Everything that was already true about the security of BGP still is.
